---
title: "About"
---

I am a PhD student in Political Science at the University of Washington, where I am also pursuing an MS in Statistics (expected June 2027). My research connects political economy with statistical methods for causal inference and uncertainty quantification.

I study how political institutions and strategic interactions shape economic development, foreign investment, and political unrest. My current work examines industrial development in China's frontier regions, contract renegotiation in Pakistan's power sector, and the reciprocal dynamics of protest and state repression.

My methodological interests include synthetic controls, conformal prediction, and hidden Markov models. I am particularly interested in learning about unobserved political and economic regimes and constructing reliable counterfactual prediction sets when those regimes change.

I also build open-source tools for teaching quantitative methods, including an [interactive multiple regression visualizer](regplot.html). My [teaching materials](teaching.html) introduce students to data science and statistics for the social sciences.

I earned a first-class BA in Philosophy, Politics, and Economics (PPE) from the University of Oxford. Alongside my studies, I was active in student journalism, serving as editor-in-chief of *The Oxford Student*. I have also worked as creative director and interviews editor at *Oxford Political Review*.

## Current projects

My current projects include [IPPs](ipps.html), a study with Hassan Aziz of Chinese sponsorship and contract renegotiation in Pakistan's power sector, and [ConformalHMM](conformalhmm.html), a method for conformal inference in synthetic controls under latent regime shifts. See [Papers](research.html) for my current research and conference presentations.
